title: Japan's hidden Christians
hookLine: after persecution, Japanese Christians kept their faith in secret for generations, with no priests

lines: A KANNON STATUE HOLDING A CHILD.
cards: Any official walking into this Japanese farmhouse would see a Buddhist home. On the family altar, a small white statue of Kannon, the Buddhist figure of mercy, holds a child.
But the family knows who she really is to them. When the doors are shut, they call her Mary. Behind a cupboard there might be a scrap of cloth, a medal, a prayer that has never been written down.
For generations, there were no priests, no churches, and the faith was against the law. And still, somehow, it was kept.

teach.h: STEP ON THE IMAGE, OR ELSE.
teach.b: You met Francis Xavier sailing to Japan earlier in this block. The faith he and others brought grew, and then Japan's rulers turned against it.
Churches were torn down, missionaries expelled, and Christians who wouldn't give up their faith were killed. Officials made people step on an image of Christ or Mary to prove they weren't Christian.
Some Christians stepped, and grieved over it afterward. And some villages went underground. They became the hidden Christians, kakure kirishitan in Japanese.
With no priests, ordinary people led. One person in a village might be the baptizer, pouring water on each newborn with the words they'd been taught. Another kept the calendar of feasts.

Their prayers, called orasho, were learned by heart and passed down from parent to child, mostly by word of mouth, until some of the Latin and Portuguese words wore smooth, like stones in a river, and the people saying them no longer knew exactly what they meant.
They kept saying them anyway. Jesus told his followers to "pray to thy Father which is in secret". These families kept that secret room for generations.

teach.h: OUR HEARTS ARE THE SAME AS YOURS.
teach.b: When Catholic priests came back to Japan, tradition tells of villagers walking into a new church in Nagasaki, and a woman whispering to the priest that their hearts were the same as his.
Some hidden communities joined the Catholic Church again. Others kept their own ways, guarded for so long. Both were choices about the same thing: what had been kept.

how: Catholics in Japan remember the hidden Christians and the martyrs, and pilgrims visit the old hidden Christian villages and churches around Nagasaki.

practice: Choose one small practice, tiny enough that nobody would notice it: one line you say on waking, one breath before you eat, a moment at the window at night.
Do it once now, slowly, as if you were handing it down to someone who will keep it after you. If you pray, make it a prayer you already know by heart; if you don't, make it a pause.
